title_idea: Everyone Blames Eve. The Verse That Assigns the Fault Uses the Singular — and Names Adam.
reveal: In the Quran's telling of the fall, the ACT of eating and the shame that follows are told entirely in the dual (they two ate, their shame appeared to them, they two began to cover themselves). But the moment the text assigns disobedience, it drops to the SINGULAR and names one person: 'and Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred' (20:121). And when the couple confess, they confess jointly, as one 'we' — 'Our Lord, WE have wronged ourselves' (7:23) — neither points at the other. The Quran refuses the blame-chain that shapes the Genesis account (Adam blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent, and the woman is named as the one who gave). Sin here is not gendered to Eve; if anything the disobedience-verb lands on Adam.
substrate: 20:121: 'fa-akalaa minhaa' (akalaa 3MD dual) ... 'badat lahumaa' (3FS) ... 'tafiqaa yakhsifaan' (tafiqaa 3MD dual) — the act and cover-up are shared/dual. Then 'wa 'asaa Aadamu rabbahu fa-ghawaa' — 'asaa (3MS SINGULAR) with the explicit named subject Aadam, then ghawaa (3MS). 7:23: 'qaalaa rabbanaa zalamnaa anfusanaa' — qaalaa (3MD dual 'they two said'), zalamnaa (1P 'we wronged'), anfusanaa ('ourselves'): joint ownership, no deflection. The dual->singular shift and the joint 1P confession are mechanically tagged in the morphology.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = recovered tafsir: al-Jalalayn glosses 20:121 'wa 'asaa Aadamu rabbahu bi'l-akl' (Adam, singular, is the one who disobeyed by eating); al-Tabari on 7:23 explicitly frames the couple's joint confession as the OPPOSITE of Iblis's response ('khilaaf jawaab al-la'een Iblees'). BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection, not a classical claim — the mufassirun contrast Adam with Iblis, not with Genesis.
overlap_note: Published: 'Adam's Tawbah and Iblis's Refusal: The Fork at the Moment of Wrong' (Adam vs Iblis) and 'Adam's Prayer: The First Words of Return' (7:23/2:37 read as a prayer). Neither reads the person/number grammar (dual act, singular fault, joint confession) or the intertextual point about who the tradition does NOT blame. Mine is the grammar-of-blame + the Genesis divergence.
imposed_check: The dual-to-singular shift is in the verb tags themselves ('akalaa/tafiqaa 3MD, then 'asaa 3MS with named subject Aadam) and al-Jalalayn already names Adam as the singular disobedient one — the reading is read OFF the text, not projected onto it.
angle: Ask a hundred people who ate the fruit first and most will say Eve. Open the Arabic: the clause that actually assigns the disobedience is singular, and the name it uses is Adam's.

title_idea: The Most Famous Test of Obedience in Scripture — and the Quran's Father Stops to Ask the Son First
reveal: In the Quran's account of the near-sacrifice, Ibrahim does not simply proceed. He tells his son the dream and turns it into a QUESTION: 'look — what do you see (think)?' (37:102). The son is not bound in silence; he answers with his own imperative — 'Father, do what you are commanded; you will find me, God willing, of the patient.' Then the very next verse uses the DUAL: 'when they had BOTH submitted' (37:103). The Quran makes the son a knowing, consenting participant. Submission becomes something shared between two wills, not imposed on one. This diverges pointedly from the Genesis binding, where the son carries the wood, asks once where the lamb is, and is bound without being consulted.
substrate: 37:102: father's speech is interrogative, not a command to the son — 'innee araa fi'l-manaami annee adhbahuka' (araa 1S 'I see/dream', adhbahu-ka 1S verb + 2MS object) then the turn to the son: 'fa'nzur maadhaa taraa' (unzur 2MS IMPV 'look', taraa 2MS IMPF 'you see/think'). Son's reply: 'if'al maa tu'mar' (if'al 2MS IMPV; tu'mar 2MS PASSIVE 'what YOU are commanded') + 'satajidunee ... min al-saabireen'. 37:103: 'fa-lammaa aslamaa' — aslamaa (3MD DUAL 'they BOTH submitted').
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = recovered tafsir: al-Jalalayn on 37:102 — 'shaawarahu li-ya'nasa bi'l-dhabhi wa yanqaada li'l-amri bihi' (he CONSULTED him so the son would be reconciled to the sacrifice and comply); al-Muyassar frames the son as 'mu'eenan lahu 'alaa taa'ati'llaah' (helping his father obey God). The consultation/consent is classical. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (Genesis 22 does not consult Isaac) = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: None found. Published articles on the decree ('Nuh and Ibrahim at the Edge of Allah's Decree') and Ibrahim's other trials do not touch the son's consent or the interrogative structure of 37:102.
imposed_check: 'fa'nzur maadhaa taraa' is literally a 2MS interrogative addressed to the son, and 'aslamaa' (37:103) is a dual verb — both are morphological facts, and al-Jalalayn independently reads it as mushaawara (consultation).
angle: The scene we hold up as the ceiling of obedience — and in the Quran's version the father pauses, mid-command, to ask the boy what HE thinks.

title_idea: Both Books Hand the Grieving Father a Bloody Shirt. In One He's Fooled. In the Other He Says 'No — You Made This Up.'
reveal: When the brothers bring Yaqub the blood-stained shirt as proof that a wolf ate Yusuf, the Quran's Yaqub does not believe it for a moment: 'Rather, your souls have enticed you to something. So beautiful patience' (12:18). He names the story a fabrication on the spot. His grief is real and lifelong (he weeps until his sight fails, 12:84), but he never despairs and never accuses — he takes his complaint only to God (12:86) and says plainly, 'I know from God what you do not know.' This is a deliberate divergence from the Genesis account, where the father accepts the bloodied coat, concludes his son was torn by a beast, and mourns inconsolably, refusing to be comforted. The Quran protects the father's prophetic dignity: he grieves without being deceived.
substrate: 12:18: 'qaala bal sawwalat lakum anfusukum amran fa-sabrun jameel' — 'bal' (rather/no) is an explicit rejection of the wolf story; 'sabrun jameel' (patience, beautiful) not despair. 12:84: 'yaa asafaa 'alaa Yusuf' + loss of sight from suppressed grief (huzn). 12:86: 'innamaa ashkoo baththee wa huznee ila'llaah wa a'lamu mina'llaahi maa laa ta'lamoon' — he complains ONLY to God and claims retained knowledge that Yusuf lives.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = recovered tafsir: al-Jalalayn on 12:18 — 'qaala Ya'qoob lammaa ra'aahu saheehan wa 'alima kadhibahum' (Yaqub, when he saw the shirt INTACT, KNEW their lie); al-Jalalayn on 12:86 glosses what he knows as 'that Yusuf's dream is true and he is alive'; al-Muyassar reads the untorn shirt as proof of the lie. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (Genesis's Jacob is deceived and inconsolable) = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: Many Yusuf-cycle articles exist (the well, Yusuf-Musa mirror, 'prison is dearer to me'), but none treat Yaqub's non-deception or his patient-not-despairing grief. This is a fresh node in a well-covered surah.
imposed_check: 'bal sawwalat lakum' in 12:18 is a direct refusal of the brothers' account in the text, and al-Jalalayn states outright that Yaqub knew the lie the instant he saw the intact shirt — the reading is grounded, not imposed.
angle: Same prop in both scriptures — a father, a dead son's bloody shirt. The gap between 'he mourned and refused all comfort' and 'he said, from the first second, you made this up' is the whole point.

title_idea: In the Bible the Queen of Sheba Goes Home Impressed. In the Quran She Says One Sentence — Aimed Past the King.
reveal: The Bible's Queen of Sheba visits Solomon, marvels at his wisdom and wealth, trades gifts, and goes home. The story is about Solomon's glory. The Quran gives her an entirely different ending: a single line of submission — and its grammar is surgical. She does not submit TO Solomon. She says 'I have submitted, WITH Solomon, TO God, Lord of the worlds' (27:44). The prepositions do the theology: 'with' (ma'a) places her ALONGSIDE the king, not beneath him; 'to God' (lillah) routes her submission straight past the throne to the One behind it. The Quran turns a story about a king's splendor into a story about a woman who sees through splendor to its source.
substrate: 27:44: 'qaalat rabbi innee zalamtu nafsee wa aslamtu MA'A Sulaymaana LILLAAHI rabbi'l-'aalameen'. zalamtu (1S 'I wronged'), aslamtu (1S, Form IV 'I submitted'). The two prepositions are the load-bearing detail: 'ma'a Sulaymaan' = WITH Solomon (not to him); 'lillaahi' = TO God. The object of her submission is God; Solomon is a fellow-submitter she stands beside.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = grounded: al-Muyassar — 'wa aslamtu ... daakhilatan fee deeni rabbi'l-'aalameen' (she entered the religion of the Lord of the worlds); al-Tabari notes Solomon built the glass court to test her intellect ('aql), and the verse's conversion-climax is the recognized reading. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (1 Kings 10 ends with admiration and gift-exchange, no submission to God) = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: Published Bilqis articles: 'The Queen Who Consulted' (her istishaara/deliberation), 'Bilqis's Throne: The Object Moved Before She Arrived', 'Bilqis and Sulayman: The Throne, the Letter, and the Question of Power'. Mine is narrowly her CLOSING LINE and the ma'a/li preposition routing + the intertextual divergence (the Bible gives her no conversion). Different focus — flag as adjacent.
imposed_check: 'ma'a' (with) and 'lillaah' (to God) are literally the two prepositions in the Uthmani text of 27:44; the object of aslamtu is God, not Solomon — this is syntax, not projection.
angle: One preposition tells you everything: she didn't say she submitted to the most powerful king alive. She said she submitted WITH him — to Someone else.

title_idea: The First Sentence Anyone Hears From Jesus in the Quran Is 'I Am the Servant of God' — and the Order of What Follows Is the Argument
reveal: When Maryam's people accuse her and she points to the infant, the child speaks — and the very first word he gives himself is not a miracle claim and not a title of majesty. It is 'servant': 'He said, I am the SERVANT of God' (19:30). Everything after it is phrased as things DONE TO him by God — God gave me the Scripture, God made me a prophet, God made me blessed. The infant's self-portrait is entirely receptive: he is the object of God's verbs, not the subject of his own power. Placed against the trajectory of later exaltation, the Quran's ordering is itself the claim — servanthood is established before prophethood, and prophethood before blessing.
substrate: 19:30: 'qaala innee 'abdu'llaah' — the first predicate is the NOUN 'abd (servant). What follows are 3MS-God-subject verbs with 1S object suffixes: 'aataani-ya'l-kitaab' (God gave me), 'ja'ala-nee nabiyyaa' (God made me a prophet), and 19:31 'ja'ala-nee mubaarakan' (God made me blessed). The speaker never takes an active verb of power for himself; he is grammatically the recipient throughout.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = grounded/explicit: al-Tabari notes the infant spoke 'mutakalliman 'an ummihi' (in defense of his mother); al-Muyassar renders 19:30 directly — 'innee 'abdu'llaah'. The first-word-is-servant and the receptive verb-chain are on the surface of the text. The contrast with later Christological exaltation and with infancy-gospel wonder-tales is the modern comparative layer, offered as reflection, and kept minimal/respectful.
overlap_note: CLOSEST published: 'A Word From Him: The Quranic Isa Before the Cradle' and 'Isa's Miracles and the Grammar of Permission'. Those treat 'a word from Him' (kalima) and the permission-grammar of the miracles ('by God's leave'). Mine is narrowly the WORD-ORDER of the cradle speech — servant, then prophet, then blessed — as a deliberately sequenced argument. Adjacent; if the panel judges it too close to 'A Word From Him', it can be cut. Flagged honestly.
imposed_check: 'abd' is literally the first predicate noun in 19:30, and the subsequent verbs are morphologically God-as-subject / Isa-as-object — the receptivity is in the grammar, not read in.
angle: Before any miracle, before any title, the first thing the Quran's infant Jesus says about himself is 'servant.' The rest of the sentence never lets him hold an active verb of power.

title_idea: In Genesis the Murdered Brother Never Speaks. In the Quran He Speaks First — and Turns the First Murder Into a Law About One Life.
reveal: In the Genesis account of Cain and Abel, the victim is silent; he never says a word, and after the killing God curses and marks the murderer. The Quran does something structurally different: it GIVES the victim a voice, and that voice is a vow of non-retaliation — 'If you stretch your hand to kill me, I will not stretch mine to kill you; I fear God' (5:28). Then it adds what Genesis has no equivalent for: a crow, sent to scratch the ground and teach the killer how to bury a body (5:31), and the killer's regret. And immediately the passage universalizes the single death into a principle: 'whoever kills one soul... it is as if he killed all mankind' (5:32). The Quran reroutes the story from a curse-narrative about the guilty to an ethics lesson centered on the victim's restraint and the worth of one life.
substrate: 5:28: victim's direct speech — 'la'in basatta ilayya yadaka li-taqtulanee maa ana bi-baasitin yadiya ilayka li-aqtulaka innee akhaafu'llaah' (basatta 2MS 'you extend', aqtula-ka 1S+2MS explicitly REFUSED via 'maa ana bi-baasit', akhaafu 1S 'I fear'). 5:31: a crow 'yabhathu fi'l-ardi' (scratches the earth) to teach burial; killer becomes 'min al-naadimeen' (the regretful). 5:32: 'man qatala nafsan ... ka-annamaa qatala'l-naasa jamee'aa' — one death universalized.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = recovered tafsir: al-Tabari and al-Muyassar read 5:28 as the victim's wa'z / maw'iza (moral admonition to his brother) — the victim's voiced non-retaliation is classical; al-Jalalayn narrates the crow and burial on 5:31. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (Genesis 4: silent Abel, God's curse/mark on Cain, no crow, no 'one soul = all souls') = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: None found — no published AyahGuide article on Cain and Abel / the two sons of Adam. Fresh node.
imposed_check: Abel's first-person refusal ('maa ana bi-baasitin yadiya ilayka') is direct speech in 5:28, the crow is in 5:31, and the universalization is the adjacent 5:32 — all consecutive text, nothing supplied from outside.
angle: The oldest murder in scripture. In one telling the dead man is silent and God curses the killer. In the other the dead man speaks first — and his line becomes the verse the Quran uses to measure the worth of any single life.

title_idea: In One Telling Adam Names the Animals. In the Other, God Names Them to Adam. Same Scene, Opposite Direction.
reveal: There is a naming scene near the start of both scriptures — but the arrow points opposite ways. In the Genesis account, Adam is the one who names the animals; naming flows outward from the human as an act of authority over creation. In the Quran, the verb is causative and God is the subject: 'and He TAUGHT Adam the names, all of them' (2:31). The names descend from God to Adam; Adam's excellence over the angels is then a gift he DEMONSTRATES, not a power he originates. The angels seal the point: 'we have no knowledge except what You taught us' (2:32). The divergence is quiet but total — it relocates the origin of human knowledge from the human to God.
substrate: 2:31: 'wa 'allama Aadama'l-asmaa'a kullahaa' — 'allama (3MS, Form II CAUSATIVE 'he taught/caused-to-know'), subject = God, object = Aadam and the names. The direction is God -> Adam. 2:32: angels' confession 'laa 'ilma lanaa illaa maa 'allamtanaa' ('allamta-naa 2MS+1P: 'what YOU taught us'). 2:33: 'anbi'hum bi-asmaa'ihim' — Adam then DISPLAYS the received knowledge. Knowledge is received, then demonstrated.
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = recovered tafsir: al-Jalalayn — God taught the names 'bi-an alqaa fee qalbihi 'ilmahaa' (by casting their knowledge into his heart); al-Muyassar — 'bayaanan li-fadli Aadam 'allamahu'llaahu asmaa'a'l-ashyaa'i kullahaa' (as a display of Adam's virtue, God taught him all the names). The God-as-teacher reading is classical. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (Genesis 2:19: Adam names the animals himself) = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: None found. AyahGuide has no article on 2:31-33 / Adam and the names, and none reading the naming as a directional (God->Adam vs Adam->creation) divergence.
imposed_check: 'allama is a Form-II causative 3MS verb with God as subject and Adam as object — the 'God teaches Adam' direction is in the morphology itself, and al-Jalalayn spells out that God placed the knowledge in Adam rather than Adam generating it.
angle: It looks like the same beat in both stories — the first human, the names of things. Flip the subject of one verb and the entire question of where knowledge comes from flips with it.

title_idea: Pharaoh's Own Magicians Are the First to Believe — and They Say It Knowing He's About to Crucify Them
reveal: In Exodus, Pharaoh's magicians fail against Moses and, at one point, concede 'this is the finger of God' — but they neither convert nor suffer for it; they simply drop out of the story. The Quran takes the same contest to a place Exodus never goes: the moment Musa's staff swallows their illusion, the sorcerers are thrown down in prostration and declare faith — 'We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun' (26:47-48). Pharaoh answers with a crucifixion threat (26:49). And they do not flinch: 'No harm — we are returning to our Lord' (26:50); 'we will never prefer you over the clear signs that have come to us — so decree whatever you will decree' (20:72). The Quran's divergence makes them the story's first believers and first martyrs: conscience defeating a tyrant inside his own court.
substrate: 26:46: 'fa-ulqiya'l-saharatu saajideen' (ulqiya PASSIVE 3MS 'they were cast down' prostrate). 26:47-48: 'aamannaa bi-rabbi'l-'aalameen, rabbi Moosaa wa Haaroon' (aamannaa 1P 'we believed'). 26:49: Pharaoh — 'la-usallibannakum ajma'een' (crucifixion threat). 26:50: 'laa dayra innaa ilaa rabbinaa munqaliboon'. 20:72: 'lan nu'thiraka 'alaa maa jaa'anaa mina'l-bayyinaat ... faqdi maa anta qaadin' (nu'thira 1P; iqdi 2MS IMPV 'decree' — defiance).
grounding: QURANIC SIDE = grounded: al-Muyassar — 'aamanoo bi'llaahi wa sajadoo lahu' (they believed in God and prostrated); al-Tabari records Pharaoh's threat to cut hands and feet and crucify them verbatim on 26:49. The conversion-under-threat is on the surface of the text. BIBLICAL-DIVERGENCE FRAMING (Exodus 8:19: magicians concede 'the finger of God' but do not convert or die) = modern comparative reading, offered as reflection.
overlap_note: Published: 'Afrigh Pour Patience: The Same Prayer From a Soldier and a Sorcerer' — that piece is about the magicians' later prayer 'pour patience over us'. Mine is a different move: the conversion-under-crucifixion-threat read as an intertextual divergence from Exodus (Pharaoh's own experts become the first believers). Partial adjacency — flagged.
imposed_check: The passive 'ulqiya ... saajideen' (26:46), the creed in 26:47-48, and Pharaoh's crucifixion threat in 26:49 are three consecutive verses; the defiant reply is direct speech in 26:50 / 20:72 — nothing is inferred beyond the text.
angle: The experts Pharaoh hired to crush Moses are the first people in the whole story to kneel — and they announce their faith already knowing the sentence is crucifixion. Exodus never lets them get that far.
